extracted.intended_audience: philosophers, students of philosophy, and scientifically-minded readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for conducting philosophy using the methods and temper of science: emphasise logical analysis, generality and a priority of propositions, piecemeal progress, and avoidance of ethical or religious prejudices and unjustified scientific generalisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should draw inspiration from science rather than religion or ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: The ethical and religious motives have been on the whole a hindrance to the progress of philosophy, and ought now to be consciously thrust aside by those who wish to discover philosophical truth; philosophy should draw its inspiration from science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Russell argues that while ethical/philosophical systems can have imaginative or practical value, their motives tend to be anthropocentric and parochial; philosophers who wish to discover truth should favour scientifically-informed motives and avoid letting ethical aims determine metaphysical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer methods, not scientific results
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two ways to base philosophy on science: emphasise the most general results of science, or study the methods of science and apply these methods (with adaptations) to philosophy. 'It is not results, but methods that can be transferred with profit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer adopting scientific methods (careful hypothesis formation, testing, logical analysis, incremental correction) rather than importing sweeping scientific generalisations as philosophical premises; examples and contrasts are given throughout the essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about using the most general scientific generalisations
rubrics_metrics.description: The most general results of science are the least certain and the most liable to be upset by subsequent research; philosophers should be chary of basing anything upon the most general scientific results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Russell illustrates this with conservation laws: erecting an empirical law into a universal a priori principle is risky because small failures in exactness can fatally undermine a philosophical edifice built on it. Use scientific generalisations prudently and only where their provisional character is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical propositions must be general (applicable to everything)
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosophical proposition must be general; it must be applicable to everything that exists or may exist, i.e., it should not concern merely particular empirical facts or parts of space-time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat the 'universe' as a special subject with predicates that cannot apply to particulars; instead, aim for distributive general propositions that hold of each individual thing or any possible world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical propositions must be a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosophical proposition must be such as can be neither proved nor disproved by empirical evidence; philosophy 'is the science of the possible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid basing philosophical claims on contingent historical, biological, or empirical facts (e.g., brain convolutions, evolution history); such special facts are irrelevant to genuinely philosophical (a priori) claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceive philosophy as logic: study logical forms and the possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy becomes indistinguishable from logic: the study of general statements about everything and the analysis/enumeration of logical forms, kinds of propositions, types of facts, and constituents of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise inventorying possibilities and analysing logical forms; this includes examining the kinds of propositions that may occur and classifying constituents of facts — tasks central to making philosophical problems precise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a piecemeal and tentative approach (successive approximations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy should be piecemeal and tentative like science, able to invent hypotheses which, even if not wholly true, remain fruitful after necessary corrections, allowing successive approximations to the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid building whole-system metaphysical edifices that if partly wrong are wholly useless; instead divide problems into manageable parts and accept provisional results that can be refined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasise analysis rather than synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of philosophy as conceived here is analysis, not synthesis: understanding general forms and dividing problems into separate questions rather than building all-encompassing systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'divide and conquer' to make philosophical problems tractable; focus on analysing logical structure and forms rather than weaving grand synthetic systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject unjustified metaphysical oneness (avoid treating the universe as a single subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception of 'the universe' as a single thing with predicates peculiar to it is mistaken; there are general propositions true of each individual thing, but no such thing as the universe as a subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of monistic, totalising metaphysical claims that rely on an assumed oneness of the world; distinguish epistemological unity (subjective) from tentative scientific unity and avoid leaping to metaphysical unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ethical/anthropocentric premises in metaphysics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical notions are essentially anthropocentric and subjective; to regard ethical notions as keys to understanding the world is to make man the centre of the universe and legislate for the universe on the basis of present human desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Russell warns that ethical motivations lead to parochial philosophies. While ethical work can be valuable in practice (ways of feeling), it should not be conflated with or used as a basis for objective philosophical theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for selection bias when generalising from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum total of what is experienced by mankind is a selection from the sum total of what exists, and any general character exhibited by this selection may be due to the manner of selecting rather than to the general character of that from which experience selects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using scientific or experiential generalisations in philosophy, carefully consider whether observed regularities arise from the selection of observed phenomena and whether they can legitimately be generalised beyond the experienced sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reify conserved quantities as persistent metaphysical entities
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an error in identifying a constant physical quantity with a persistent entity; energy is a function of a physical system, not a thing or substance persisting through change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating quantities like mass or energy as metaphysical substances whose persistence is an a priori presupposition of science; recognize that such concepts are partly conventional and mathematical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalise the observed simplicity of laws to all undiscovered laws
rubrics_metrics.description: What is surprising in physics is not the existence of general laws but their extreme simplicity; however simplicity has been part cause of their discovery and gives no ground for supposing other undiscovered laws are equally simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers should not assume that the simplicity of known laws implies universal simplicity; the discovery process favours simple laws, so simplicity is a selection effect, not evidence of universal simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose philosophical problems into logically distinct subproblems
rubrics_metrics.description: Many supposed single philosophical problems are actually confusions of distinct problems requiring different methods (e.g., logic, physics, and theory of knowledge in Kant's problem of space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and separate the logical, empirical (physical), and epistemological elements of a problem and treat each with the appropriate methods: logic for exact solutions, physics for empirical questions, and careful analysis for theory of knowledge.
